title: Emerging Evidence on Online Preventive Parenting Interventions and Children’s Outcomes: A Systematic Review
abstract: Abstract Background Online preventive parenting interventions have been increasingly recognized as an important platform in recent years, broadening accessibility and eliminating barriers related to time and resources for attending intervention services. Objective This study sought to explore the effects of online preventive parenting interventions on child psychological and behavioral outcomes while examining moderators and mediators underlying these interventions, as well as program engagement. Method The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Randomized controlled trial studies of preventive interventions directly targeting parents of children aged between 3 and 12 with measured child outcomes were included in the review. Results The final sample included 14 studies focusing on 11 online interventions. Primary outcomes for most studies included child behavior problems and mental health. Most studies reported positive intervention effects at post-intervention, while several reported nonsignificant changes. Few studies examined relevant moderating and mediating processes. Of the 14 studies reviewed, 11 provided information about program engagement, typically through module completion and session attendance. Conclusions Longitudinal tests of mechanisms of change and of the subgroups that benefit most from online interventions would help clarify how and for whom these programs work. Combining multiple informants, such as parent, child, teacher, and observer reports, would strengthen the evidence on child outcomes. Research on optimal dosage, the role of human support, and effective, sustainable delivery formats may also be informative.
